nameStory: The leopard slug gets its spotted name from the dark blotches and spots scattered across its light grey body, creating a pattern reminiscent of a leopard's coat. It's also called the 'great grey slug' because it's one of the largest slugs you'll encounter, measuring up to 8 inches long when fully extended.
description: The leopard slug is a large, impressive mollusk that can stretch 4-8 inches long when moving. Its body is typically light grey or grey-brown with distinctive dark spots and blotches, though the exact pattern varies quite a bit from individual to individual. This hefty slug is actually a European native that made its way to New England in the 1800s and has been thriving here ever since. You'll notice a pronounced ridge or 'keel' running along the back portion of its body.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Impressively large slug that stretches 4-8 inches when extended, with a robust, elongated body that feels firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Spotted Pattern
idTips.description: Light grey or grey-brown base color decorated with irregular dark spots and blotches that create a leopard-like appearance

idTips.label: Back Ridge
idTips.description: Prominent keel or ridge running along the back half of the body, giving it a slightly triangular cross-section when viewed from behind

idTips.label: Mucus Trail
idTips.description: Leaves a thick, silvery slime trail that feels distinctly sticky and stringy compared to smaller slugs

idTips.label: Tentacle Length
idTips.description: Four tentacles on the head with the upper pair being noticeably long and dark-tipped, retracting quickly when touched

habitat: Look for leopard slugs in moist, shaded areas around human habitation like gardens, compost piles, under decks, and in basements or cellars. They favor areas with plenty of organic matter and often hide under logs, stones, or in leaf litter during the day. Unlike many native slugs, they're quite comfortable around buildings and developed areas.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often seen after spring rains moving across sidewalks and garden paths, feeding on emerging vegetation and organic matter.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid summer nights, retreating to cool, moist hiding spots during hot days. Look for their distinctive thick slime trails on garden walls.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity period as they feed heavily before winter, often found near compost piles and fallen leaves. This is when you're most likely to witness their spectacular aerial mating displays.
seasonality.winter: Hibernate in protected spots like basement corners, under deep leaf litter, or in root cellars, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Leopard slugs perform one of nature's most extraordinary mating rituals - they hang suspended in mid-air from a thick rope of their own mucus, sometimes dangling 20 feet down from tree branches while intertwining their bodies in a spectacular spiral dance that can last for hours.
confusionNotes: Often confused with large garden slugs, but leopard slugs are much bigger and have that distinctive spotted pattern and back ridge. Memory trick: if it's longer than your thumb and has spots, it's likely a leopard slug - most other slugs in New England are smaller and more uniformly colored.
contextualKnowledge: This is actually an introduced species from Europe that arrived in Philadelphia in 1867 and has been spreading ever since. Despite being non-native, leopard slugs are generally considered beneficial because they often eat other slugs and dead plant matter rather than focusing on live garden plants like some smaller slug species.
compareHints: As the only Limax species commonly found in New England, leopard slugs are easily distinguished from other large slugs by their spotted pattern and pronounced back keel. Most other large slugs in the region lack both the distinctive leopard-like markings and the prominent ridge along the back half of the body.
